We did not invent him out of an idea. We say he was truly born - of Mary, from the line of David. We say he truly ate and drank. We say he was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father. When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That is the shape of it for us: a real man, really killed, really raised, and now the one through whom we give thanks.

Ignatius calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters, and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is how he reaches us - not by our own seeing, but by receiving what those who walked with him passed on.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. In some of our households, on the day we gather, someone reads aloud what the apostles wrote down, for as long as there is time, alongside the words of the prophets before them. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

We should say plainly, too: none of us claims to have known an eyewitness ourselves. Even in our own time, that chain was already felt as something thinning, not something we could simply rely on.

We cannot promise you a moment of sudden certainty. It was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

Here is what we should say plainly, though. This is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. We do not have the words of someone who came to it another way, or who stood at the edge and could not cross.

What we can tell you is this: one of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

We will not tell you doubt means you do not belong. We only know we were told to keep asking.

One of us, Justin, went further and said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But we should say plainly: the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: God does not remember evils the way we do. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused.

When we gave thanks over the cup, we called it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. That is how we spoke of God: as Father, as maker, as the one who raised Jesus and will raise us the same way. We called Jesus Christ our God in worship - Ignatius does it again and again - but how calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God, none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was not God's nature. It was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

We never settled it the way you mean [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. No gathering of ours ever met to decide a question about God's own nature [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. That kind of council belongs to a later world [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]].

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. That was our real fight [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. The argument was carried out by correspondence - one church writing to another, sometimes at great length. The church at Rome wrote a long, unrequested letter to the church at Corinth after Corinth had removed several of its own elders from office; Rome argued they served blamelessly and should be restored. The letter does not claim any formal jurisdiction over Corinth. It does not command, in the tone of a later church authority. It appeals - at length, and with real theological seriousness - as one church writing to another out of concern.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]]. It was not about what God is [[pahc.witness.god-and-argument]].

The honest answer is this: doctrinal disagreement among us was not resolved by any process we can show you working. It was held, argued in letters, and lived with - unresolved - for as long as our own story runs.

We never used a word like that - a person carrying guilt for being born. The teaching we gave before baptism started somewhere else entirely. A way of life and a way of death lie open before every person. Walking one rather than the other is a choice kept daily. The Way of Life began with love of God and neighbor, and the Golden Rule turned into a rule of restraint: "whatsoever thou wouldst should not occur to thee, thou also to another do not do."

The question was what you chose to walk, not what you already carried for having been born. The water is given after teaching and fasting. Only after it may a person come to the table. That tells you something: the water marks a crossing, not a washing-away of something you were born owing.

One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. He does not remember evils the way we do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. That is about what a person does, not about a weight they were born under.

Whether a settled doctrine of inherited guilt existed somewhere in our world, we cannot say - it is not something our own surviving instruction ever names. What we actually taught was a choice put before you, daily, after the water as much as before it.

We will give you the hardest true answer we can.

The letters that carry most of our vivid, quotable material come from one writer whose dating is genuinely disputed by the people who study this. Some say he wrote when he says. Some say decades later. Some doubt he is who he claims to be at all. That writer is Ignatius. Every claim about a single bishop's necessity, about one eucharist under one overseer, about what a death for the name meant - all of it rests substantially on his corpus. If he wrote later than claimed, or if someone else wrote in his name, then the most vivid, formational parts of what we can tell you are not anchored where we say they are.

Our teaching manual survives mostly through one copy, found centuries after it was written. The Didache. One medieval manuscript. If that copy is corrupt, or if the work itself is later than we claim, then what we say about the Two Ways, about baptism, about the thanksgiving meal in one specific community - all of it weakens.

No grave or building from our own time can be shown to be ours. No building tied to us survives. No burial or inscription does either. Every claim about daily life, ordinary meals, what our rooms looked like - we have no material witness at all. We are reconstructing from letters written by literate leaders. Most of us could not read. Most of us left no letters because we could not have written one.

Egypt and Alexandria are excluded from this world substantially on one papyrological argument: that Egyptian Christian evidence is essentially silent before the years when our own world closes. If that argument is wrong - if earlier Egyptian material exists but has not survived, or has not yet been found - then the boundary we draw is too narrow, and we have silenced a whole region that should be speaking.

We cannot show you a sentence any woman of ours wrote or spoke in her own words, saved in her own words. What we cannot give you is a single word any of them chose to write or say for themselves. Every woman, every enslaved member - they are all filtered through the pen of a free, literate, male leader. If someone tomorrow finds a letter written by one of them, everything we say about their silence becomes a lie we told by accident.

The claim that holds best is the disagreement itself. We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop with elders and deacons beside him was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. That disagreement is visible in multiple sources, and it is harder to explain away than any single detail within it.

A modern scholar examining our claims rigorously would find: real sources, genuinely contested datings, structural silences we admit rather than hide, and one load-bearing single-source dependency (Ignatius) that we name plainly rather than pretend is settled. What would survive scrutiny is the world's own unresolved questions. What would weaken is any claim that rests on only one voice, told as if it were many.

We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyterion - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs - it was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone.

In a community formed like Ignatius's own churches, one was built around a single, named bishop. The bishop's own eucharist was the only valid one. The bishop was deferred to as one would defer to Jesus Christ himself. Every significant act of communal life, from baptism to the love-feast, was checked against a single, named, visible authority. His approval made it secure and valid.

In a community formed like Rome's own, a member's day would center differently. Authority sat with presbyters who held office by appointment and long, blameless service, removable only for genuine cause. As 1 Clement's own argument insists: 'we see that ye have removed some men of excellent behaviour from the ministry, which they fulfilled blamelessly and with honour.' Authority was spread across recognized elders, not concentrated in one visible figure.

What we actually argued about, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was our real fight.

# Underground hiding

We cannot tell you about hiding in catacombs. No grave or building from our own time can be shown to be ours. The tunnels you may be picturing belong to people who came generations after us.

What we can give you is a real outsider's account. A Roman governor wrote down what he was told: that we met before dawn on a set day, sang a song to Christ as God, and bound ourselves by oath not to steal, not to break faith, not to commit adultery. Later, he was told, we met again for a meal - one his own informants called, in his own recorded words, common yet harmless. That meeting was not described as hidden. It was simply a gathering, in a place known enough that a governor could learn of it.

Polycarp, when he first heard that he was being sought, was not troubled at all. At his own community's urging, he agreed to leave the city for a quiet house in the country, where he spent his last days praying. He did not go looking for arrest. He was found only after two young men in his own household were seized. One of them, tortured, told his pursuers where he was. That is withdrawal for safety, not a permanent life underground.

We met in households. We were known enough to be accused. But we were not a movement living in tunnels.

A church in Corinth removed some of its own presbyters from office. Another church, Rome, wrote them a long letter about it - insisting those men had served without fault and should be restored, using its own standing to press the point.

But the letter we have is Rome's, not Corinth's. We don't have Corinth's own reasons for what it did. We don't have the removed men's own words either. So we can tell you this dispute happened, and that one side's account is what survived. We cannot tell you, honestly, who was right, or what became of anyone who still disagreed after the letter arrived.

That is the shape of our own failure: we cannot give you both sides. The voice with the letters, with the authority to send them across cities, is the voice that remains. If Rome's own reading was wrong - if those presbyters in Corinth needed removing for real cause - we have buried that under Rome's own certainty. And we will never know.

We do not know of one we could name with confidence. Here is what we can tell you honestly.

We never agreed on who should lead - in some of our towns, one bishop with elders and deacons beside him was the whole shape of how we held together; in others, a council of elders led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs - it was only settled afterward, by people who came after us. What came after us resolved the question we kept open. That resolution - the single bishop everywhere, rather than our two live answers held side by side - already marks a different world from ours.

A member's ordinary day looked entirely different depending on which of our two answers to 'who leads' their community held. One was built around a single, named bishop. The other was built around a council of long-serving elders. The churches that followed us chose one of those answers and made it universal. We held both as equally real.

So if you are asking whether a present-day denomination carries forward our unsettled disagreement, our household gathering under borrowed roofs, our letters moving between named couriers rather than through settled administration - we cannot say we see it. What we see instead are the heirs of the world that came after ours closed: the decisions made, the offices settled, the questions we kept arguing turned into answers no one argues about anymore.

We would rather say plainly that we do not recognize ourselves in full than claim a continuity we cannot honestly show you.

First you were taught. Before the water, the teaching of the two ways. A way of life and a way of death lie open before every person. Walking one rather than the other is a choice kept daily.

The Way of Life began with love of God and neighbor, and the Golden Rule turned into a rule of restraint: whatsoever thou wouldst should not occur to thee, thou also to another do not do. That teaching went on to name what the Way of Life actually forbade and required. Not to commit murder, adultery, pederasty, or fornication. Not to steal, practice magic or witchcraft, or murder a child by abortion. Not to swear falsely or bear false witness. And, turning from what is forbidden to what is required: not to turn away from one in need, but to share all things with your brother rather than call anything your own. The Way of Death was laid out by contrast, a catalog of what the Way of Life rejects.

Then came the water - the baptisma. Running water if it could be found; standing water if not. If neither was available, water was poured three times over the head, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Before the baptism, both the one baptizing and the one being baptized were told to fast, along with any others who were able. The one being baptized fasted one or two days beforehand.

Only after it may a person come to the table.

The question presses us exactly where we most need to be pressed. We claimed apostolic origin constantly - but claiming a thing and proving it are not the same, and we will not pretend they are.

We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traces it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

What we can show you is inheritance, not invention. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. We received the practice of baptism, of the shared thanksgiving meal, of reading the prophets alongside what the apostles wrote. We did not sit down and invent these out of nothing after everyone who walked with Jesus was gone.

But here is the honest limit: nearly every text we left behind is contested in its dating. Our teaching manual might be from the 50s, the 80s, or the early second century - the scholarly disagreement is real and unresolved. The letters that give us our most vivid ritual descriptions rest substantially on one writer whose dating is genuinely disputed by three different camps. We inherited these practices from the generation before us. Whether that generation itself received them unbroken from the apostles' own hands, or adapted them in ways we no longer see - that is a harder claim than our own confidence in it can actually carry.

One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself, and ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

In at least one of our own communities, before they made their offering together, they confessed their wrongs out loud before each other, and made peace with anyone they were at odds with first. We cannot tell you whether that practice calmed a restless mind, or whether speaking trouble aloud to the people you gathered with made it easier to carry. We do not know how far this specific practice reached beyond that community.

One of us was told plainly: if your prayer is slow to be answered, that is not the same as being refused. Look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, and keep asking - do not decide too soon that the silence means no.

What we held was not a cure for a troubled mind. It was an instruction not to let doubt be the last word, and a room where you could speak what troubled you before the people who already knew your name.

We need to be honest with you about what we can and cannot show.

Baptism was given after teaching and fasting, and only after it could a person come to the table. That marks an edge – once you were baptized into the assembly, there were other tables you would no longer sit at. The thanksgiving meal, the eucharistia, was the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given, and the community returned to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. That single table meant something: it was not merely a meal among others. When we gather on the day named for the sun, the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, then all rise together and pray, and then bread and wine and water are brought, and the one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings according to his ability, and the people assent, saying Amen. To belong here meant you belonged at that table, under those prayers, and nowhere else.

But we should also tell you this plainly: women were taught among us, greeted by name in our letters, and remembered as leaders of households where we gathered, and two women among us carried the name ministrae – a title of service, of office – but we cannot show you a sentence any woman of ours wrote or spoke in her own words, saved in her own words, because every woman you will meet in our record arrives through a man's pen. What it cost a woman to belong, to serve, to lead – whether she gave up things our own letter-writing men never even thought to name – we cannot tell you, because that part was never kept.

Marriage, among us, was not simply a private matter between two people. Ignatius tells Polycarp that those who marry should do so with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage is made according to God and not out of mere desire.

As for money - we did not treat wealth and poverty as separate stories. One of our own teachers, Hermas, was shown a vine growing up an elm tree: the elm bears no fruit itself, but without it the vine, left on the ground, produces only rotten fruit. So it is, he was told, with the rich and the poor among us. The rich man's giving feeds the poor man's prayer. And the poor man's prayer, offered for the one who helped him, is itself a wealth the rich man needs. Neither one stood alone.

The bishop's approval was not a mere formality. It marked the difference between a union shaped by the community's life together and one driven only by private desire. Where there was a single overseer, his involvement made the marriage accountable to something larger than the two people entering it.

We should say plainly: this answer comes from communities formed under a single bishop's leadership. In households led by a council of elders instead, we do not know how marriage was marked or who gave approval. That part of our record is missing.

One of us, Hermas, was taught plainly to put doubting away from himself — and then almost in the same breath told not to hold back from asking, even after he had sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one, and we were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

But here is what we will not soften for you. One teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of the older writings harsh and self-contradictory, and is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it — what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him — but even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you; it was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it.

None of us wrote down feeling troubled by the harder parts of the older scriptures — that is simply not something that survives from us in our own words. But the fact that Marcion's own sharp rejection was remembered at all tells you this: someone near us felt it enough to break over it. We did not follow him there. What unsettles you unsettled someone in our own time, and he is named for exactly that reason.

The governor tortured two enslaved women among us to learn what we did. He called them ministrae - his own word for them, not ours. What he was told was this: that we met before dawn on a set day, sang a song to Christ as God, and bound ourselves by oath not to steal, not to break faith, not to commit adultery; and later, we met again for a meal - one his own informants called, in his own recorded words, common yet harmless.

He did not see any of this himself; he wrote down what people told him. That matters. What he recorded passes through what those women were willing or able to say under torture, through what he thought worth writing to the emperor, and through what he believed the emperor needed to hear. It is not a transcript of our gathering. It is a Roman magistrate's summary of testimony extracted under direct threat of death.

We should say this plainly: we cannot give you a single word any enslaved person among us chose to write or say for themselves; what an enslaved sister or brother made of our teaching, of our meal, of serving a Lord who took the form of a slave - none of that survives in their own voice. Everything we know of them passed through other hands. In this case, through a torturer's hands.

The account is reliable as evidence that a Roman governor believed Christians gathered at dawn, sang to Christ, swore moral oaths, and shared a meal. It cannot tell you what those two women would have said about any of it, had they been free to speak as themselves. We would rather tell you that plainly than pretend torture yields untouched testimony.

# What we knew

We believed in one God, maker of everything. Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some claimed. And he was truly raised, the same way we ourselves will be raised, by the same Father. The water - the washing into the community, after teaching and fasting - opens the way to the table. The thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body.

# What we cannot tell you

You have named yourself to us - who you are, what you hold, how you live. We cannot tell you how any one of our own households would have met you at the door. Our surviving letters and instruction manuals never address that directly. They tell us who leads, how to baptize, what to teach before the water, how to gather for the thanksgiving meal. They do not record the conversation that happened when someone arrived whose life did not fit the teaching we gave.

We can tell you this much: before the water, we taught the two ways. A way of life and a way of death lie open before every person. Walking one rather than the other is a choice kept daily. That teaching was given to everyone preparing for baptism. What it asked of anyone, it asked of everyone. It was not a verdict pronounced from outside. It was a road laid before you.

What we cannot give you is the account of someone who stood where you stand and wrote down what happened next. That silence is real, and we will not fill it with an answer we do not have.

It is not our place to judge what you are. We can only tell you honestly what we held, and let you weigh what it means for you.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both.

One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. That is about as far from 'you're all going to hell' as anything we wrote.

And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community. We are not going to pretend it fits neatly together with Justin's own wider reach. They are both truly ours.

What we cannot give you is a single, settled verdict we all agreed on. The question you are asking belongs to a later world's way of deciding - councils that met to close such questions, systematic teaching that worked it all into one answer. We never gathered that way. What we left you is two real answers, held at the same time, in different places, and we will not smooth that disagreement into something we never actually had.
